sections.title_en: From the Best of the Produce
sections.body_en:
It is a mitzva to separate terumot and ma'asrot from the best part of the produce, as it is stated (Bamidbar 18:32): "when you set apart its best (ḥelbo) from it" – "ḥelbo" is its best part. And if there is no kohen or Levi there, and there is a concern that by the time he brings the good, ripe produce to the kohen and the Levi it will spoil, it is preferable that he separate from produce that will keep for a long time, even though it is not the very best. If he transgressed and separated the inferior produce, what he did is done and his produce is permitted to be eaten (Mishna Terumot 2:4-6; Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 5:1).

Today, when we are all considered impure and the kohanim cannot eat the terumot, all produce is considered entirely inferior with regard to terumot, and therefore it is permitted le-khatḥila (from the outset) to separate terumot from the inferior produce. But ma'aser rishon for the Levi and ma'aser ani must be separated from the good produce (SA YD 331:52; Bi'ur Ha-Gra 95; and see below in halakhot 10-11).1

The mitzva is to separate terumot and ma'asrot from produce of the same species, and if one separated terumah from produce of one species on behalf of another species, his terumah is void, and he must separate terumah again from produce of the same species. This is the rule: whatever are kilayim (forbidden mixtures) with one another – such that if they are vegetables, it is forbidden to sow them intermingled, and if they are trees, it is forbidden to graft them onto one another – they are two species, and one does not separate terumah from one on behalf of the other, even from the superior species on behalf of the less superior one. But if there is no prohibition of kilayim between them, it is permitted to separate terumah from one variety on behalf of another variety of the same species. For example, all kinds of grapes in their various colors, and all kinds of cabbage in their various colors – they are one species. Likewise, peach and nectarine – one species. But oranges and grapefruits – two species (Mishna Terumot 2:6; Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 5:2-3; Mishpat Kohen 25; above 3, note 4).

notes_en.en:
Today, when the kohanim do not eat terumah, one may separate terumot from liquid wine lees on behalf of wine, according to the quantity of the liquid part in the lees, and some have estimated this at sixty percent (Divrei David vol. 4, YD 61). Mishpetei Eretz 8:23 was concerned about the difficulty of estimating, but his words are puzzling, since one can resolve the doubt by estimating stringently.
The Sages decreed that if one separated terumot and ma'asrot from ears of grain on behalf of wheat [kernels], or from olives on behalf of oil, or from grapes on behalf of wine, what he did is void, since he caused a loss to the kohanim and Levites, who would have to take the trouble to make wheat from the ears, oil from the olives, and wine from the grapes. He must separate terumot and ma'asrot from them again after their processing is complete (Mishna Terumot 1:4; Rambam 5:18). And if the kohen and the Levi agreed to receive their gifts from the ears, olives and grapes – after the fact what he did is done and the produce is rectified (Rash, Rosh and Radbaz). According to our master Rav Kook, today, when in any case the kohanim cannot eat their terumah, even without the consent of the kohen and the Levi, after the fact the produce is rectified. Some disagreed with regard to the ma'aser (see Ha-ma'aser Ve-ha-teruma 5, se'if katan 14, and Ma'adanei Eretz, Terumot 5:18:3).
One who buys grapes for eating and separated terumot and ma'asrot from them, and afterward changed his mind and decided to make them into wine, need not separate terumot and ma'asrot from them again (Mishna Terumot 1:9; Rambam 5:20). If he bought them for eating, and before he separated terumot and ma'asrot he changed his mind and decided to make them into wine, it is forbidden to eat from them even casually (akhilat arai), since they already became obligated in terumot and ma'asrot when he bought them for eating (Ma'adanei Eretz, Terumot 1:14:7).

sections.title_en: From Obligated Produce on Behalf of Exempt Produce, and Different Levels of Obligation
sections.body_en:
One does not separate from produce that is exempt from terumot and ma'asrot, such as produce from outside the Land and produce from which terumot and ma'asrot have already been separated, on behalf of produce that is obligated in terumot and ma'asrot. And likewise the reverse: one does not separate from obligated produce on behalf of exempt produce. And if one separated – he has done nothing, and he must separate terumot and ma'asrot again from the obligated produce (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 5:12).

Produce from two different places, regarding both of which there is a doubt whether they have been tithed – one should not separate from one on behalf of the other, lest he separate from tithed produce on behalf of untithed produce or the reverse.

One should not separate from produce that is obligated in terumot and ma'asrot by rabbinic law on behalf of produce that is obligated by Torah law. And likewise the reverse: one should not separate from produce obligated by Torah law on behalf of produce obligated by rabbinic law.

Produce obligated by Torah law is produce that the owner of the field grew for the needs of his household, or produce that a person bought from the owner of the field before its processing was complete, and completed its processing himself for the needs of his household. Produce obligated by rabbinic law is produce that the owner of the field grew in order to sell it, as well as produce that grew in an unperforated pot. (In the note the law of one who erred and separated from one on behalf of the other will be explained.)2

One does not separate from produce whose obligation depends on one rabbinic enactment on behalf of produce whose obligation depends on two rabbinic enactments, and likewise the reverse. That is, even though today the entire obligation of terumot and ma'asrot is rabbinic (below 12:11), one should not separate from grapes that a person harvested for eating at home on behalf of grapes that a person harvested for sale. After the fact, if one separated from one on behalf of the other – he has fulfilled his obligation.3

notes_en.en:
If one separated from produce obligated by Torah law on behalf of produce obligated by rabbinic law, he has rectified the produce that is obligated by rabbinic law. But the produce that was separated as terumot and ma'asrot requires rectification, for since by Torah law one did not need to separate terumot and ma'asrot [from the rabbinically obligated produce], it turns out that by Torah law he separated from obligated produce on behalf of exempt produce and did nothing, and therefore the produce he separated as terumot and ma'asrot has remained tevel. According to the Rambam (Hilkhot Terumot 5:16), one must separate terumot and ma'asrot for it from elsewhere. And Ri explained (Tosafot, Yevamot 89b, s.v. "mi-makom") that if he separates from it on behalf of itself, he may mistakenly eat its remainder, whereas beforehand he had made it terumot and ma'asrot. (And according to Rashi on Kiddushin 46b and the Meiri, he may separate from it on behalf of itself, for there is no concern that he will eat its remainder.)
If one separated from produce obligated in terumot and ma'asrot by rabbinic law on behalf of produce obligated by Torah law, the terumot and ma'asrot take effect by rabbinic law; but since by Torah law it accomplished nothing, since he separated from exempt produce on behalf of obligated produce, he must separate terumot and ma'asrot again from the produce obligated by Torah law (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 5:14).

According to the Turei Even (Megilla 19b), it is permitted le-khatḥila to separate from produce with one rabbinic obligation on behalf of produce with two, and the reverse. But according to the majority of poskim it is forbidden, and so wrote the Maharam of Rothenburg (Responsum 423), cited in the Beit Yosef (330:6), and so wrote the Mishneh La-melekh, Sha'arei Tzedek, Ha-ma'aser Ve-ha-teruma, and Kerem Tziyon. However, after the fact one has fulfilled the obligation, since in practice the obligation of both types is rabbinic (Torat Ha-aretz; Ḥallat Leḥem; Mishpetei Eretz 8, note 30; below 12, note 21). Le-khatḥila one should be stringent also not to separate from produce with two rabbinic factors on behalf of produce with three rabbinic factors, and when necessary one may be lenient. In practice these are the common cases, for the Aḥaronim agree that today terumot and ma'asrot are rabbinic, and according to the majority of poskim most produce is obligated by rabbinic law (except for grain, wine and oil), and consequently, when part of the produce is designated for the home and part for sale, it is a case of two rabbinic factors on behalf of three rabbinic factors (Rav Azriel Ariel, "Hafrashat Terumot U-ma'asrot Ba-ma'arekhet Ha-tziburit," p. 53).

sections.body_en:
It is a mitzva to separate terumah gedola from the mukaf (adjacent produce), that is, from produce that is near and adjacent to each other, such that it can be encompassed together. After the fact, one who separates terumah gedola not from the mukaf has fulfilled his mitzva (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 3:17, 20). Since terumat ma'aser is also called terumah, the Sages were accustomed to separate terumat ma'aser from the mukaf as well.4

If the produce is lying in an open field, one should bring it close together (SA YD 325:2). Produce lying within one room, even when part of it is on one side and part on the other side, the walls of the room make it mukaf. And even if it is lying in open vessels, the room combines it (SA 331:26).

When one is about to pack the produce in boxes, bottles or closed sacks, le-khatḥila one should separate terumot and ma'asrot from it beforehand, since some hold that fixed packaging separates between the foods and they are not considered mukaf together. When necessary, one may bring them close to each other and separate terumah also on behalf of the produce inside the packaging. However, barrels or bottles of wine, in which the wine continues to age and improve – since people are careful that they remain closed so as not to damage the wine, what is inside each barrel or bottle is separate unto itself and is not considered mukaf with its fellow, and therefore one must separate terumah on behalf of the wine before sealing it in barrels or bottles. Or else they should separate terumah from each and every barrel and each and every bottle after they are opened (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 3:18; SA 331:26).

For the sake of a mitzva, it is permitted to separate not from the mukaf. For example, one who knows that tevel produce is going to be brought to him on Shabbat or Yom Tov may, while it is still day, separate terumot and ma'asrot from produce in his possession on behalf of the produce that is going to be brought to him (Yevamot 93a). Likewise, one who mistakenly gave his fellow tevel produce, and is unable to notify him to tithe it, should tithe it from produce in his own possession, in order to save his fellow from eating tevel (Eruvin 32a).5

notes_en.en:
In Mishna Ḥalla 1:9 it is explained that terumah gedola must be taken from the mukaf. And in Mishna Bikkurim 2:5 it is explained that terumat ma'aser need not be taken from the mukaf, as it is stated (Bamidbar 18:28): "from all your tithes that you take" – even "one in Yehuda and one in the Galil" (Yerushalmi Terumot 2:1). According to many, the mitzva to separate terumah from the mukaf is of Torah origin, as it is stated: "from it" (Bamidbar 18:27-32; Tosafot, Rabbeinu Tam, Rash, Rid, Tosafot Ha-Rosh, Rashba, Ran and Gra). And some hold that the mitzva is rabbinic, because one separates terumah gedola by estimate, according to the measures the Sages instituted – one-fortieth, one-fiftieth or one-sixtieth (above 7:2) – and in order to estimate well, he must see all his produce before him (Radbaz; Shakh YD 331:49-50; and so it is implied by the Ra'avad). In any event, according to all opinions, if one separated terumah not from the mukaf – he has fulfilled his obligation, for even if the mitzva is of Torah origin, it is like the mitzva to separate from the best, where after the fact, if he separated from the inferior, he has fulfilled his obligation. And according to my teacher and master Rav Yisraeli, today there is no obligation to separate from the mukaf, for even according to those who hold that the law of mukaf is of Torah origin, its purpose is so that he can estimate how much to separate, and today, when one separates any amount whatsoever for terumah, there is no need for this (Ha-Torah Ve-ha-aretz vol. 3, p. 134). As for the reason for the mitzva, one can say that the idea is that the terumah should rise up from within the whole of the produce, and thereby the imprint of holiness remains in all the produce from within which the terumah rose up.
In the Bavli, Gittin 30b, it is explained that "ḥaverim" (Torah scholars) are careful to separate terumat ma'aser too from the mukaf, because it too is called terumah. However, for terumah gedola this is an obligation, while for terumat ma'aser it is a custom that "ḥaverim" were particular about, and therefore one need not be particular about all the laws of mukaf, but only that he see them before him (Rambam 3:20; Rash, Ramban, Rashba). And according to Tosafot (Gittin 30b, s.v. "ve-khi"), for terumah gedola it is a Torah mitzva to separate from the mukaf, and the Sages instituted it for terumat ma'aser as well. Regarding ma'asrot, it was ruled in the Rambam (Hilkhot Ma'aser 1:6) and in the SA (331:71) that they need not be separated from the mukaf.

It is permitted to separate terumah on behalf of oil that is in closed jugs, but one should not separate on behalf of wine that is in sealed jugs (Yerushalmi Ma'aser Sheni 3:6; Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 3:18; SA 331:26). This is because with wine people are particular that it be closed in order to preserve its quality (Rash Sirilio). And according to the Radbaz, with oil one is lenient because it is packed for a short time, and with wine one is stringent because it is usually sealed for a long time. Accordingly, when the produce is in preserve cans or in large sacks, one should be stringent not to separate terumot on behalf of it (Ḥut Shani; Mishpetei Eretz 12:9-10). Rav Eliyahu ruled similarly. However, when necessary one may rely on the opinion of the Rash Sirilio, that only with wine must one be stringent, and separate terumah on behalf of the produce inside closed cans and bags. And one may add to this the opinion of Rav Yisraeli, who holds that today it is permitted le-khatḥila to separate terumah not from the mukaf. And when there is a concern that people will stumble by eating tevel, even with bottles of wine it is permitted to separate terumah not from the mukaf.
I wrote that in order to fulfill the law of mukaf there is no need for the produce or the open vessels to touch each other, because this is the view of the overwhelming majority of the poskim. So wrote the Rambam (Hilkhot Terumot 3:18), Rash, Rosh, Rashba, Tur, SA 331:26; Arukh Ha-shulḥan, Zera'im 62:10. However, according to Rabbeinu Tam, when the produce is in an open place without walls surrounding it, it must touch, and so wrote the Gra (325:8) regarding open vessels, that they must touch each other (Mishpetei Eretz 12:8 was stringent in accordance with the minority opinions).

sections.title_en: How One Measures, and the Law of One Who Errs
sections.body_en:
In separating ma'asrot and terumat ma'aser, one should try to be precise, so as not to separate more than a tenth and not to separate less than a tenth. To this end one must measure produce whose volume is usually measured, and count produce that is usually counted, and best of all is to calculate by weight, which is the most precise (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 3:11; Hilkhot Ma'aser 1:14). After the fact, when it is not possible to weigh, measure or count the produce, he should separate the ma'asrot by estimate. And even if he errs greatly, as long as he intended to separate the proper measure and erred in the way people sometimes err – he has fulfilled his mitzva. But le-khatḥila the Sages instructed (Avot 1:16): "Do not tithe excessively by estimate."6

The accepted practice today (as will be explained further on) is that one does not actually separate produce for the ma'asrot, but only determines that a tenth of the produce lying on the south or north side shall be ma'aser. In this way the quantity of produce designated for ma'aser is precise. Afterward one gives their value to the Levi and to the poor person, and the produce of the ma'aser sheni one redeems on a peruta. However, the terumot, which are sacred, must actually be separated, and afterward one wraps them in order to place them respectfully in the garbage bin. For the terumot one must separate more than one-hundredth of the produce – one-hundredth for "terumat ma'aser," and the part beyond the hundredth for "terumah gedola." If one separated for the terumot exactly one-hundredth or less, it turns out that he did not separate "terumah gedola," since the terumah gedola is the part "beyond one-hundredth." And since it never occurred to him not to separate "terumah gedola" first, everything he did is void, and he must separate terumot and ma'asrot again in order (see Mirkevet Ha-mishneh and Yeshu'ot Malko on Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 13:19; Ma'adanei Eretz, Terumot 3:23:8).

The separation of terumot and ma'asrot has the same law as other vows and consecrations: if one regretted them, he may ask a Sage, together with two other people, to annul the separation for him according to the rules of annulling vows, and thereby the produce returns to its state of tevel (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 4:17. The same law applies to ḥalla, below 10:13 [?]).7

notes_en.en:
Tosefta (Demai 8:10) and Yerushalmi (Demai 5:2): "One who diminishes his tithes – his tithes are rectified and his produce is spoiled; one who exceeds his tithes – his tithes are spoiled and his produce is rectified." That is, if one separated less than a tenth, his separation stands, and he must complete it and separate more produce in order to reach a tenth (Ribmatz and Rosh on Mishna Terumot 4:1; Ramban; Ra'avad on Hilkhot Ma'aser 1:15; Gra 331:125). And some say that his separation is void, since it did not contain a tenth (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 3:7; Hilkhot Ma'aser 1:15; SA 331:77). And if he erred and separated more than a tenth, all the produce on whose behalf he separated ma'aser is rectified, but the produce he separated as "ma'aser rishon" is not rectified, since the produce beyond the tenth is tevel from which ma'aser sheni or ma'aser ani must be separated (Ramban and Ritva on Gittin 31a). And some say that there is no way to rectify it (Meiri).
Some are stringent (see Mishpetei Eretz 18, note 18) based on what they inferred from the Rishonim and Aḥaronim mentioned, that the case is one who separated by estimate and therefore diminished or exceeded. However, besides the fact that their inference is not compelling and is contrary to reason, many wrote explicitly that everything they said about one who diminishes or exceeds his tithes refers to one who intentionally exceeded or diminished the tithe. But if it came out that way by mistake, even if he separated by estimate, he has fulfilled his obligation. So wrote the Rash (Terumot 1:7), Tosafot (Gittin 31a, s.v. "nitelet"), Kaftor Va-feraḥ 24; Sha'arei Tzedek 10:11; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 61:3. And so it appears from the words of Rabbi Yosei in the Yerushalmi, Demai 5:2, that the beit din stipulated "up to the point where the mind errs." That is, an error that people commonly make is not considered an error that impairs the tithes, for the Torah commanded human beings to separate terumot and ma'asrot, and they are incapable of absolute precision. Therefore, even if they separated by estimate and erred greatly, as long as it is an error that some people commonly make, they have fulfilled their obligation. For even if they use the most precise scale, they will not succeed in calculating the net weight of each fruit, since it is hard to calculate how much peel and seeds it contains, and even with the scale itself it is impossible to be precise to a tenth of a gram. All the more so they will not succeed in being precise when they tithe by measure or number, for certainly about half of people will separate more than a tenth and about half will separate less. Therefore, one must say that an error that people commonly make does not impair the mitzva, but le-khatḥila they said not to separate by estimate, in order to come closer to precision.

After people have already eaten from the produce, one should not annul the separation, so as not to turn those who ate from it into eaters of tevel (Rema 323:1; Shakh 6). And according to the Ḥatam Sofer (YD 253), when necessary it is permitted to annul the separation even after they have eaten, since the eaters bear no sin, as they ate in a permitted manner. And see Ha-ma'aser Ve-ha-teruma 4, se'if katan 27. After he has given the terumah to a kohen or the ma'aser to a Levi, he can no longer annul the separation (Rosh and Ran on Nedarim 59a; Mishpat Kohen 39:2; Ha-ma'aser Ve-ha-teruma 4:20). When he separates a second time, some say that he should not recite a blessing, since the first blessing is effective for the second separation, and since it is a case of doubt regarding blessings, one should not recite the blessing (Rashash, Nedarim 59a).

sections.title_en: The Law of Terumot in Our Times
sections.body_en:
Today, the kohanim may not eat pure terumah, since everyone is considered impure with the impurity of the dead, and we have no possibility of becoming purified from this impurity without the sprinkling of the water of the ashes of the red heifer. When the terumah is pure, it is forbidden to burn it or destroy it; rather, one must leave it until it decomposes on its own, or store it away by burial. When the terumah is impure, it is a mitzva to burn it so that people will not come to eat from it. However, it is difficult to burn it, and sometimes it is pure and it is forbidden to burn it, and a person does not always know whether it is pure. Therefore, the custom is to wrap the terumah and place it in the garbage bin, whether it is impure or pure, for in this way there is no concern that people will come to eat from it, and also one does not treat it with disrespect, since one places it wrapped.

When large quantities of terumah are involved, as long as it has not become impure, since it is forbidden to destroy it, one must leave it at the edges of the field until it decomposes on its own. And when there is a concern that people will come to eat it, it is proper to bury it or cover it a little with earth. And if it has become impure, it is a mitzva to burn it, and one may also bury it or compress it in a manner that it will be destroyed and people will not come to eat it.8

Terumah produce that became mixed with ḥullin produce of the same species is nullified in a hundred. And if they became mixed, one species with a different species, and he cannot separate the terumah from the mixture, for example because everything was mashed, the terumah is nullified in sixty. And if there was not the proportion necessary for the terumah to be nullified, one must treat the entire mixture as terumah (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 13:1-2). When necessary, just as vows are annulled, so too one may ask a Sage regarding the separation of the terumot and ma'asrot and annul it (as explained in the previous halakha).

notes_en.en:
It is forbidden to cause a loss to pure terumah (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 12:1), and Sefer Ha-teruma wrote that so that people will not stumble with it, one should bury it. So wrote the Semag, Tur 331:19; Yam Shel Shlomo; Taz 331:9. Regarding impure terumah, they said in the Mishna (Temura 33b) that it is burned. According to Rashi, Rid and Rav Ovadya of Bartenura, the meaning is that one must destroy it so that people will not stumble with it. And according to Tosafot, Ramban, Rashba and Ritva, one must specifically burn it, like the law of disqualified sacrifices (Shabbat 25a). Similarly, we learned (above 2, note 3) regarding orla and kilei ha-kerem (mixed growth of the vineyard), that there is a dispute whether one must specifically burn them or whether the main thing is that people not stumble with them. And the Ḥatam Sofer (OḤ 180) wrote that if one burns it, he fulfills a mitzva, but there is no obligation to do so. In any case, one must be careful that people not stumble by eating it.
In practice, the custom is to wrap the terumah, whether it is pure or impure, and place it thus in the garbage bin. And apparently the custom is not to be stringent to burn it because of the effort involved, and because of the concern that by the time they find a way to burn it, people will mistakenly eat it. In addition, the law of terumah today is rabbinic, and in a case of doubt the halakha follows Rashi and those who agree with him; and even when the terumah is of Torah origin, Tosafot wrote (Shabbat 25a) that there is a doubt whether the law of burning is of Torah origin. The reason for wrapping it is so that it not be treated with disrespect, for we have learned that it is forbidden to treat terumah with disrespect, even when it is impure (Yerushalmi Shevi'it 8:2; Ha-ma'aser Ve-ha-teruma 1, note 39). Some argue that if it is pure, by placing it inside a bag in the garbage bin one causes its destruction, since it rots quickly in the bag, and furthermore that one causes the sanitation workers to destroy it, by its being placed in the central garbage container, where the bag will tear and the terumah will be treated with disrespect and become disgusting. However, in practice, there is no certainty that terumah rots faster in a bag (see Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it 4, note 2), and there is also a reasonable chance that the bag will not tear in the central garbage container; if so, it is a case of a doubtful indirect cause (safek gerama) and an unintended outcome (davar she-eino mitkaven), and there is no prohibition in this.
When large quantities of pure terumah produce are involved, and there is a concern that people will come to eat them, some suggested spraying them with a repellent odor, for since it can be washed off, it does not cause the produce to be destroyed. But one should not make compost from the produce in a manner that hastens its rotting (see Ha-Torah Ve-ha-aretz vol. 4, in the article by Rav Azriel Ariel).

sections.body_en:
As we have learned (7:7), even though it is forbidden for a kohen to eat impure terumah, it is desirable that he benefit from it by way of burning. If the terumah is produce – he should fire the oven with it, and if it is oil – he should light the lamp with it. When the kohen lights for himself an oven for heating with impure terumah produce, or a lamp with impure terumah oil, it is also permitted for a Yisrael to benefit from it, for "a lamp for one is a lamp for a hundred." And even if the kohen afterward went on his way, the Yisrael may continue to benefit from the lamp or the oven that the kohen lit (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 11:18). Just as it is forbidden to burn on Yom Tov the meat of sacrifices that became impure, so it is forbidden to burn impure terumah on Yom Tov; therefore, it is forbidden to light a lamp on Yom Tov with oil of impure terumah (Shabbat 24b).9

At the time when the kohanim could become pure and would eat terumah, the kohen was permitted to feed his animal only produce that was not fit for human consumption. And today, when it is forbidden for kohanim to eat terumah, a kohen is permitted to feed his livestock or his animals with terumah produce, whether the terumah is pure or impure. So that the terumah should not go to waste for nothing, some have the custom of transferring ownership of their livestock to a kohen who is a Torah scholar, and thus they can feed them the terumah that they separate for him. Afterward they settle accounts with the kohen and pay him what they saved in buying food for the animals.10

notes_en.en: When there is a possibility that the kohen will be able to benefit from burning the terumah, it is good to render the produce impure before its processing is complete (Tur; Rema 331:19), but after the processing is complete it is forbidden to render it impure (Shakh 35). Some are lenient to render the produce impure after the processing is complete and before the separation of terumah, but after its separation, according to all opinions it is forbidden (Kaftor Va-feraḥ, Radbaz). Susceptibility to impurity is created when the produce becomes wet with one of the seven liquids (above 7:7), and afterward, if a Jew touches it with his hand or if it touches an impure vessel – it becomes impure. The simple way to render produce impure is to sprinkle on it water that first passed over the hand of a Jew, for then the water becomes impure and immediately renders the produce impure. But the hand of a living gentile does not render the water impure. And even though the Sages decreed upon gentiles the impurity of a zav and zava, one does not burn terumah on account of this, since it is a rabbinic impurity that has no basis in the Torah (Nidda 34a; Rambam, Hilkhot Mishkav U-moshav 2:10. However, a corpse, whether of a gentile or of a Jew, renders impure by contact as an av avot ha-tum'a (primary source of impurity) by Torah law, and with regard to tent impurity (tum'at ohel) – a Jewish corpse renders impure and a gentile corpse does not render impure – Rambam, Hilkhot Tum'at Met 1:12-13).

It is explained in the Sifra (Emor 5:6) and in Tanna De-vei Eliyahu Rabba 14 that it is forbidden to give an animal terumah that is fit for human consumption, because one thereby causes it a loss, and only terumah from produce that is fit for humans in pressing circumstances, such as vetch, may be given to a kohen's animal (and what is not fit at all for human consumption is exempt from terumot and ma'asrot). So wrote the Rash, Rav Ovadya of Bartenura (Terumot 11:9), Ra'avad, Ritva and Kaftor Va-feraḥ. On the other hand, according to Tosafot and the Rashba, a kohen may give his animal to eat pure terumah that is fit for human consumption, but if it became impure, he must burn it and it is forbidden to feed it to his animal. And according to the Rambam (Hilkhot Terumot 9:7) and Rashi, even impure terumah may be given to an animal, for in this way too it can be eliminated. Accordingly, according to the Rambam and Rashi, a kohen may feed his animal pure and impure terumah; according to Tosafot and the Rashba, he may feed it pure terumah but seemingly impure is forbidden; and according to the Rash and those who agree with him, seemingly it is forbidden to feed it either pure or impure. However, Maharam Ḥaviv wrote in Responsa Kol Gadol 56 that today, when the kohanim do not eat terumah, even according to the Rash and those who agree with him it is permitted le-khatḥila to feed it to their animals, since there is no loss in this. And Rav Frank added (Har Tzvi, Zera'im 1:101) that even impure terumah is good to feed to a kohen's animal, since in this way the kohen benefits from it while eliminating it from the world. So too wrote Rav Herzog (Ketavim U-fesakim 3:32). And according to our master Rav [Kook] (Mishpat Kohen 38:1-2), the one who is lenient has a basis to rely upon. And some say that it is proper not to feed terumah to an animal by hand, but rather to place the terumah before it, farther away than is customary, so that even according to those who are stringent, its loss will be only through gerama (indirect causation) (Rav Shmuel Salant; Ḥazon Ovadya, Terumot U-ma'asrot p. 236).

sections.title_en: A Kohen and a Levi Who Have Produce
sections.body_en:
Kohanim and Levites who have produce must separate terumot and ma'asrot from it like all Jews. But the kohen keeps the terumot in his possession and treats them with sanctity as required, and he also keeps the "ma'aser rishon" in his possession, for since he too is from the tribe of Levi, he has no obligation to bring it to a Levi. And a Levi who has produce separates terumot and ma'asrot from it as required, and keeps the "ma'aser rishon" for himself, and the terumot he gives to a kohen (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 1:3-4).

A kohen and a Levi who bought produce from a Yisrael after the work of its gathering was completed – the Sages penalized them, so that they do not separate terumot and ma'aser rishon for themselves but rather give them to other kohanim and Levites, so that they will not come to buy tevel produce from Yisraelim and deprive their brethren by taking the terumot and ma'aser rishon for themselves. However, if they bought the produce before its processing was complete, the terumot and ma'aser rishon are not taken from them (Yerushalmi Pe'ah 1:5; Rambam there 6:15).

Generally, the Levites would separate "terumat ma'aser" from the ma'aser they received, and they would also choose to which kohen to give it. But if the Yisrael wishes, he may separate "terumat ma'aser" from the ma'aser rishon that he separated for the Levi, and give it to a kohen together with the "terumah gedola," even though he thereby takes away from the Levi the right to choose to which kohen to give the "terumat ma'aser" from his ma'aser (Gittin 31a; Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 3:12). Today, in order to prevent mishaps and forgetfulness, it is preferable that the Yisrael who separates the ma'aser immediately separate the "terumat ma'aser" as well, and place the terumot in the garbage bin, respectfully wrapped.

As we have learned (above 7:8), it is a mitzva to give "ma'aser rishon" to a Levi. And although many hold that following the penalty that Ezra imposed on the Levites, it is permitted to give it to a kohen as well (Tosafot and Tur), since some hold that after the destruction of the Temple the penalty lapsed and the mitzva reverted to giving it specifically to a Levi, it is proper to satisfy all the poskim and give it specifically to a Levi (Rambam; SA YD 331:19; Mishpat Kohen 56).

Some argue that today there is no mitzva to give the "ma'aser rishon" to a Levi. And although it is obligatory to separate it by fixing a place for it – that it be on the north side of the produce and the like – in practice one need not give it. This is because, according to their argument, as a result of the upheavals of the exiles, the presumption of lineage was lost, and no person can prove that he is a member of the tribe of Levi, and consequently there is no obligation to give him the ma'aser (cited in Maharit 1:85). And some argue that as long as the presumption of lineage is not examined in a beit din, one may not rely on a person's word with regard to receiving gifts, so that there not be a proliferation of swindlers who will claim that they are Levites in order to receive the ma'aser (cited in Ḥazon Ish, Shevi'it 5:12). And some have the custom to be lenient on the basis of these arguments.

However, according to the overwhelming majority of the poskim, one must give "ma'aser rishon" to a Levi, because we rely on the tradition. Just as we rely on the tradition regarding kohanim, and give them the money of pidyon ha-ben (redemption of firstborn sons), and they go up to the platform to recite Birkat Kohanim, so too one should rely on the presumptive status of the Levites. And since in any case a person must separate ma'aser kesafim (a tithe of income), he should give the "ma'aser rishon" to a Levi who is a Torah scholar, and count it as part of "ma'aser kesafim" (as explained in the following halakhot).11

notes_en.en: Some have the custom to be lenient, and have relied on the opinion of the Ḥazon Ish (Mitzvot Ha-aretz 11:2; Ha-aretz U-mitzvoteha, Terumot U-ma'asrot 5:4). However, the overwhelming majority of the poskim wrote that one must give the ma'aser to a Levi. So wrote the Shulḥan Arukh (YD 331:19), Responsa Maharit (1:85), the Shelah (Sha'ar Ha-otiyot, letter kuf, Kedushat Ha-akhila); Responsa of Rabbi Betzalel Ashkenazi 2; Eretz Ḥayim (Sitehon) 331:4; Har Tzvi (Zera'im 1:107); Siddur Olat Re'iya (vol. 1, p. 350). And so Rav Yehuda Amiḥai summarized in practice, and wrote that so ruled Rav Yisraeli and Rav Eliyahu (Ha-Torah Ve-ha-aretz vol. 4). Likewise, we have learned that one relies on the presumptive status of kehuna with regard to pidyon ha-ben (Ḥatam Sofer, end of 291; Arukh Ha-shulḥan YD 305:30; Sedei Ḥemed, Ma'arekhet Kaf, kelal 92; and unlike She'ilat Ya'avetz 1:155). Even the Ḥazon Ish himself did not decide to be lenient in this, and he himself was accustomed to give it to a Levi (Derekh Emuna, Terumot 6, Tziyun Ha-halakha 78). And since in any case a person must give "ma'aser kesafim," even for those who doubt whether one must give ma'aser rishon to a Levi, it is proper to give the ma'aser to a Levi who is a Torah scholar, and to count it as ma'aser kesafim, as will be explained in the next halakha. And at a time of great hardship, when it is difficult to demand that the farmers separate ma'aser for the Levi, one may ask the Levi to act generously, and after the ma'aser rishon has been transferred to him, to ask that he transfer it back to the owner of the produce, as many kohanim do with the money of pidyon ha-ben. So ruled our master Rav [Kook], as related in "Eleh Mas'ei" p. 118 and Igrot Ha-re'iya, letter 119.

sections.body_en:
In years 1, 2, 4 and 5 of the shemita cycle, one separates ma'aser sheni, and in years 3 and 6, ma'aser ani. Since the laws of ma'aser rishon and ma'aser ani are the same – they are ḥullin and are given in our times as in the past – we will deal first with the laws of ma'aser ani, and then complete the halakhot pertaining to both of these tithes.

A poor person too must separate "ma'aser ani" from his produce, and unlike a kohen and a Levi, who separate terumot and ma'aser rishon and keep them for themselves, the poor person must give the "ma'aser ani" to another poor person (Ḥullin 131b). Also a poor person who bought tevel produce must give the "ma'aser ani" to another poor person (Pe'at Ha-shulḥan 5, se'if katan 25). If his brother or his son was poor, as long as he is not separating in the field, he may give him all of it (above 7:11). Since this is so, it is preferable that he give the "ma'aser ani" to his relatives, for in the mitzva of tzedaka a person must give precedence to his relatives.

A poor person who is entitled to receive "ma'aser ani" is one who cannot obtain his basic needs according to what is accepted in that time and place. It seems that in a country that provides welfare budgets for the elderly and needy, the poor are those who are around the bottom tenth of the society in which they live, and in a country that does not provide welfare budgets, the percentage of the poor can reach a fifth of the entire public; but it is not plausible that more than a tenth or a fifth of the entire public would be considered poor, unless we are speaking of years of famine.

One may give "ma'aser ani" produce or its monetary value to a gabbai tzedaka (charity administrator) for the needs of the poor (Mishna Ma'aser Sheni 5:9). Likewise, one may give "ma'aser ani" to a yeshiva that supports young men and avreikhim (married yeshiva students) who live modestly and whose parents do not have money to support them. And even though young men and avreikhim who are helped by their parents and live comfortably also study there, they should direct that the "ma'aser ani" money be allocated to the support of the poor young men and avreikhim.

After the poor person has received the "ma'aser ani" produce, he may eat it or sell it and buy whatever he wishes with the proceeds. But it is forbidden to take it out of the Land, as it is stated (Devarim 26:12): "that they may eat within your gates and be satisfied" (Sifrei there; Arukh Ha-shulḥan, Zera'im 14:18). If he took it out, after the fact he may eat it outside the Land (see Pe'at Ha-shulḥan 12, se'if katan 27).

sections.title_en: The Manner of Giving the Ma'aser to the Levi and the Poor in Practice
sections.body_en:
The "ma'aser rishon" for the Levi, and the "ma'aser ani" that is separated in the third and sixth years – these are the tithes that are eaten by their recipients even today, because they are ḥullin and need not be eaten in purity. The measure of each of these tithes is about 9% of the produce. For we have learned that today one separates any amount whatsoever for "terumah gedola"; it turns out that even after its separation, the amount of produce remains as it was. Afterward one separates "ma'aser rishon" for the Levi, and from it one separates a tenth for the kohen, which is called "terumat ma'aser." It turns out that the part belonging to the Levi is about 9% of the produce. Afterward, in the third and sixth years, one separates "ma'aser ani" from the remaining produce, and its measure too is about 9% of all the produce, for after subtracting the "ma'aser rishon," 90% of the produce remains, and a tenth of that is 9%.

When the owner of the produce can bring the ma'aser produce to the Levi and the poor person – very good. However, today it is very difficult to distribute the ma'aser produce. For the mitzva is that when the owner of the produce finishes gathering his produce from the field, he separates terumot and ma'asrot, and the kohen, the Levi and the poor person come to him, and he gives each one his portion. And if they did not come, the Sages instituted that the owner of the field or his worker should bring it to their homes, and they pay him the customary wage for this (above 7:5). Today, most fruit growers are farmers who have large areas and whose yield is enormous, and if the farmer brings all his ma'aser produce to one Levi and one poor person, they will have no place to store it and will not know how to sell it. And if the farmers hire workers to distribute the ma'aser produce to Levites and poor people, in a quantity suited to the household consumption of each one, the payment they would pay for this distribution would be higher than the monetary value of the ma'aser produce they would receive. And then the Levites and the poor would prefer that the ma'aser produce, which entails a high payment for its transport, not be brought to them.

In order to fulfill the mitzva in a beneficial way, in accordance with its purpose, the owners of the produce should separate the ma'asrot for the Levi and the poor person, and afterward buy the produce from them with money, and give them the money. Le-khatḥila the owner of the produce must perform an act of acquisition (kinyan) so that the "ma'aser rishon" produce passes into the possession of a particular Levi, and the "ma'aser ani" produce into the possession of a particular poor person, and afterward buy the produce from them (as explained in the note). Or he can do this by means of a prior arrangement, by way of "makirei levi'ya" and "makirei ani" (acquaintances of a Levi or poor person) (as explained in the next halakha). After the fact, even when they did not perform an act of acquisition and did not arrange this in advance, the owner of the produce must convert the ma'aser produce into money, and afterward give this sum to the Levi and the poor person. And even though he did not receive permission from a particular Levi and a particular poor person to convert the produce into money, this falls under the category of returning a lost object, for by buying the ma'aser produce he saves it from destruction (Ḥullin 134b; Rambam, Hilkhot Bikkurim 9:16).12

notes_en.en:
The mitzva is to give the ma'aser produce itself to the Levi (and likewise to the poor person), and not to pay him a sum of money for it (Maharik Korkos in a responsum in Avkat Rokhel 16; Pri Ḥadash YD 61:16; Maḥazik Berakha 10, regarding the priestly gifts). However, since reality today has changed greatly, it is difficult to bring the ma'aser produce to the Levites. For in the past, when about 90% of a person's work was devoted to obtaining food, the price of food was very high relative to the customary payment for hours of work, and it was worthwhile for the Levites to come to the fields to receive the ma'aser for their household consumption. And if they did not come, they would bring the produce to their homes, and the recipients paid for the transport, since the price of transport was lower than the price of the produce. But today it is not worthwhile for a Levi to invest in traveling to the fields for one type of produce for his household consumption, nor is it worthwhile for him to pay for transporting the produce to his home. For as modern agriculture developed, the prices of produce fell, until a family can buy basic food for a month for a sum equal to a tenth of an average salary. And even this price is mainly for the transport and marketing of the food, and not for the food itself, whose production cost has fallen greatly thanks to developments and technology. Therefore, the cost of transporting produce from the field to the home of one person for his household consumption is more expensive than the value of the produce he will receive. And one may not demand that the farmer bring all the ma'aser to one Levi, since his obligation is to give each one only enough to satisfy him. And even if he brings it, the Levi will not know what to do with an enormous quantity of produce, since he does not know how to store it and market it. And since if the produce remains in the field it will spoil, one must save it by redeeming it for money.
Le-khatḥila one must transfer ownership of the ma'aser produce to the Levi and the poor person, and for this purpose one must make use of another person who will perform an act of acquisition on it on their behalf. And even though the Levi and the poor person for whom he acquires it do not know about this, since it is a benefit for them, they will certainly agree that the produce be acquired on their behalf, for "one may confer a benefit on a person in his absence" (Gittin 30a). When the produce is plentiful and difficult to lift, they should perform the acquisition by means of renting a courtyard (kinyan agav), whereby the person who acquires on their behalf pays a shekel for a particular place of a tefaḥ by a tefaḥ for a day, and along with the courtyard he acquires the ma'aser produce on their behalf (see SA ḤM 202). In pressing circumstances one may also acquire by means of kinyan sudar (symbolic exchange), whereby he gives a garment or a vessel to the owner of the produce, and in place of the garment or vessel he acquires the produce on their behalf (Minḥat Shlomo 62:15).
If there is no other person there through whom the produce can be transferred to the Levi and the poor person, by virtue of the mitzva of returning a lost object the owner of the produce may convert the produce into money, as explained in Ḥullin 134b; Rambam, Hilkhot Bikkurim 9:16; SA 61:10, regarding the priestly gifts. In addition, the Radbaz (1:340) defended the custom that many followed of paying money instead of giving the gifts.

sections.title_en: Giving the Ma'asrot in Practice to Acquaintances among Levites and the Poor
sections.body_en:
One of the good ways of fulfilling the mitzva of giving the ma'asrot in our day is that the owner of the produce arranges in advance with a Levi who is a Torah scholar that he will receive the "ma'aser rishon" from him, and gives the Levi a monetary loan against the ma'asrot that he will separate in the coming year. Through this, this Levi becomes his "makir levi'ya," that is, a Levi known as the one who receives his ma'asrot, and then, immediately after the separation of the ma'aser, the ma'aser produce passes into his possession without the need for an act of acquisition. And each time the owner of the produce separates ma'aser, he should calculate its value and deduct it from the loan that the Levi owes him, and thereby the ma'aser produce returns to his possession. When the price of the ma'aser produce reaches the value of the loan, the loan is erased, and the owner of the produce again gives an additional loan to the Levi, and again deducts the value of the ma'asrot from the sum of the loan. One can do the same with a poor person regarding "ma'aser ani" (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 7:5-6).

For repaying the loan, the price of the produce is calculated according to the cheap market rate of the produce, so that if at the beginning of the season its price is high and in the middle of the season it is low, the price of the produce should be calculated throughout the season according to its low rate. And there is no ribbit (prohibited interest) in this, since this is not an ordinary loan, but a loan that serves as an advance payment for the ma'aser produce, and its repayment depends on the value of the ma'aser produce, and if there is no ma'aser produce against it, the loan will be erased (Gittin 30a; Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 7:7).13

notes_en.en:
Just as one can give the loan to a Levi or a poor person, so one can give it to a yeshiva that grants stipends to avreikhim who are Levites or poor, or that employs rabbis who are Levites.
The price that the farmer must pay for the ma'aser produce is its value in the field at the end of the gathering, without any further handling, since the owner of the produce need not trade in the ma'aser produce on behalf of the Levi. It turns out that if the farmer receives from the wholesaler between 1,000 and 3,000 NIS per ton of produce, it may be that the price of a ton of ma'aser produce is about 700 NIS. First, because one calculates according to the cheap rate, which is 1,000 NIS. Second, the farmer need not handle the Levi's ma'aser produce or find a buyer; rather, the Levi must come to the field to take it. And perhaps the owner of the field, thanks to his connections and experience, succeeds in selling the produce for 1,000 NIS, but another person would obtain about 700 NIS; it turns out, then, that this is the true value of the produce. In any case, this complex calculation must be carried out honestly and with fear of Heaven, so as not to deprive the Levi and the poor person. And when the farmer has doubts, he should consult a rabbi or an expert who will calculate the price without bias toward any side. And in the merit of the ma'asrot he will merit to become wealthy.
Of course, the ma'aser rishon and ma'aser ani should be counted as ma'aser kesafim and ḥomesh (a fifth of income), for ma'aser kesafim and ḥomesh were instituted as a substitute for terumot and ma'asrot from a person's other earnings. However, it is possible that the expense of the ma'aser for the Levi and the poor person will be greater, since they are given from all the produce, without deducting the expenses for the work of growing it, irrigating it and fertilizing it, whereas ma'aser kesafim is separated only from net profit. On the other hand, since the ma'aser produce is assessed according to its low value as explained above, it turns out that the ma'aser for the Levi is not from all the earnings, but a tenth of about a third of the price the farmer receives for them, and perhaps even less. And even in the third and sixth years, in which he must give an additional tithe to the poor, it is not certain that this amounts to more than a fifth of his profits, which is the measure one should give for the choicest fulfillment of the mitzva (SA YD 249:1). (And if he gives the ma'asrot to a yeshiva, he will receive tax refunds.) In any event, according to the law, even if the cost of terumot and ma'asrot is more than a fifth, the obligation remains in place. And when all the farmers fulfill the mitzva properly, everyone profits from the fulfillment of the mitzva. However, in a situation in which there are farmers who do not fulfill the mitzva properly, one should not demand of the religious farmers, who must compete with them, to give more than a fifth of their profits, and in pressing circumstances one should not demand of them to give more than a net tenth of their profits, like the law of ma'aser kesafim. And if the ma'asrot amount to a higher sum, one should ask the Levi and the poor person to act kindly toward the farmer and return to him part of the produce they received. And in great hardship they were lenient to ask the Levi and the poor person to forgo almost the entire ma'aser (as explained in note 11).
The matter of "makirei kehuna u-levi'ya" is explained in Gittin 30a. And in the Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 7:6, it is explained that there are also "makirei aniyim." Some were uncertain how the Levi becomes a "makir" (Mishpetei Eretz 17:10), and it seems obvious that the uncertainty applies to a small loan, but one who gave a significant loan to a Levi at the beginning of the season for his ma'asrot – the Levi thereby becomes a "makir." The "makir" acquires the ma'aser without an act of acquisition, because the other Levites withdraw from the ma'aser (Rashi there), or because the owner of the produce committed himself to this to the "makir," and it is forbidden for him to break his word (Tosafot, Bava Batra 123b, s.v. "ha-kha").
Even if the owner of the produce forgot to give an additional loan to the makir levi'ya, the ma'aser produce passes into his possession, for since he has already become accustomed to giving him the ma'aser, he has become his "makir levi'ya," who acquires his ma'aser rishon without an act of acquisition. And he should hurry to pay the Levi the value of the ma'aser, and give him a loan again in order to continue fulfilling the giving of the ma'aser on the basis of that loan. A farmer who merits to give large ma'asrot may designate several Levites who will receive the ma'aser from him, and le-khatḥila it is preferable to do so through a yeshiva or a gabbai tzedaka. And see the Harḥavot.

sections.body_en:
The mitzva of eating "ma'aser sheni" produce in purity within the walls of Jerusalem depends on the existence of the Temple (above 7:9); therefore today, when the Temple is destroyed, even if we could become purified from the impurity of the dead, we would have no possibility of eating the "ma'aser sheni" produce. Nevertheless, it is obligatory to separate terumot and ma'asrot, including "ma'aser sheni," because the mitzva of separation does not depend on the existence of the Temple (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser Sheni 2:1). However, there is no need for the "ma'aser sheni" produce to go to waste, because the Torah established that the "ma'aser sheni" produce can be redeemed for money, and thereby the sanctity passes to the money and the produce is permitted to all. And although the Torah's commandment is to redeem it for its value plus a fifth, after the fact, if one redeemed it for a peruta, the produce is deconsecrated. And since today the redemption money goes to waste, le-khatḥila one may redeem it for one peruta, and this is indeed what it is worth, since it is impossible to benefit from it (Rambam 2:2; 4:18).

With less than the value of a peruta it is impossible to redeem the produce, because it has no significance, and therefore it is impossible to perform an acquisition or redemption with it. The value of a peruta is the value of 1/45 of a gram of silver. Since the price of silver is subject to fluctuations, the value of the peruta rises and falls (in recent years the value of the peruta has generally been about four to five agorot).

When necessary, one may redeem "ma'aser sheni" produce onto food worth a peruta, wrap it, and place it respectfully in the garbage bin, just as one places terumah. But le-khatḥila one should redeem "ma'aser sheni" produce onto money.

A person who wishes to redeem "ma'aser sheni" produce from time to time onto a peruta must designate a coin for this, and if the price of the peruta remains about five agorot, as it is today, he can redeem onto a five-shekel coin one hundred times, and onto a ten-shekel coin two hundred times. In order to remember that this is the coin designated for this, it is proper to mark it with a sticker.14

This is the order of the redemption: after finishing the separation, one recites the blessing: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to redeem ma'aser sheni," and says: "This ma'aser sheni, it and its fifth, is deconsecrated onto one peruta of the coin that I have designated for the redemption of ma'aser sheni." And if he deconsecrates it onto food, he says: "This ma'aser sheni, it and its fifth, is deconsecrated onto this food," and places it wrapped in the garbage bin, so that it will not be treated with disrespect.

notes_en.en: The value of a peruta is the weight of half a barleycorn of refined silver (SA 331:134). According to Rav Ḥayim Na'eh it is 1/40 of a gram. So too wrote the Ḥazon Ish (ḤM 16:30). However, according to the comparison of the peruta to other coins and to the barleycorn, it turns out that the weight of the peruta is 1/45 of the value of a gram of silver (Middot Ve-shiurei Torah 22:12; 25:4). In practice, the price of silver metal is subject to fluctuations. For decades the price of the peruta was less than 3 agorot. In 5760 (2000) it began to rise; in 5765 (2005) it reached about 5 agorot; and in 5772 (2012) it reached a peak of 13 agorot, and since then it has fallen again. In the last three years its price has been between 4 and 5 agorot (written in 5778 [2018]).

sections.body_en:
When one redeems "ma'aser sheni" onto money, one must redeem it onto a coin that is in circulation in that place, and not onto a coin that is not in circulation there, since it is not considered money there (Rambam 4:9-10).

A person may permit his family members and friends to redeem "ma'aser sheni" produce that they have onto the coin that he designated for this, provided that he estimates that they will not exceed the number of perutot that his coin is worth. And if he is in doubt, he can designate two coins for this, one of ten shekels and one of five shekels (and it is good to stick them together in order to mark them), and give everyone permission to deconsecrate onto a peruta of the large coin; and every so often, as needed, he deconsecrates all the perutot of the large coin onto one peruta of the small coin. He should do so until the time of "bi'ur ma'asrot" (removal of tithes) arrives, at which time he deconsecrates all the perutot of the large and small coins onto a piece of fruit, or wine or oil, worth a peruta. Afterward he can use these coins again for the coming years. If he redeemed the perutot onto a piece of fruit or food, he should place it wrapped respectfully in the garbage bin. And if he redeemed onto wine or oil, he should pour them into the sink, but not into the toilet.15

When a person redeems his "ma'aser sheni" produce onto his fellow's coin, he does not add a fifth, but says: "This ma'aser sheni shall be deconsecrated onto a peruta of the coin that so-and-so designated for the redemption of ma'aser sheni" (Rambam 5:1, 8).

When "ma'aser sheni" produce is worth less than four perutot, since the value of the fifth is less than the value of a peruta, one does not add a fifth, and he says: "This ma'aser sheni shall be deconsecrated onto a peruta of the coin that I have designated for the redemption of ma'aser sheni" (Rambam 5:4). If he erred and added a fifth in a case where he did not need to add it – he has fulfilled his obligation.16

notes_en.en:
Le-khatḥila they would not deconsecrate a coin onto a coin, but after the fact, if they deconsecrated, it is deconsecrated (Rambam 4:5); therefore today, when in any case it is impossible to eat the "ma'aser sheni" produce, it is permitted le-khatḥila to deconsecrate money onto money (Kaftor Va-feraḥ ch. 40). And one may deconsecrate coin onto coin and back again several times. Some preferred not to deconsecrate money onto money, and ruled to destroy the money onto which the "ma'aser sheni" produce was deconsecrated (Ḥazon Ish, Demai 3:12; Mishpetei Eretz 15, notes 55-58). But since it is difficult to destroy a coin, and it is also against the law, it is better to redeem coin onto coin several times until the time of bi'ur ma'asrot, and this is the accepted custom, and no one holds that this deconsecration has no validity.
When the time of bi'ur ma'asrot arrives, he should redeem all the perutot onto food. Some say that one should not redeem money onto food (Ḥazon Ish, Demai 3:10). However, the opinion of the overwhelming majority of the poskim is that one redeems money onto food. And some say that one should not redeem onto food that has become susceptible to impurity (Tosafot, Kiddushin 56a, s.v. "be-mezid"). And this is proper le-khatḥila. However, after the fact one may deconsecrate even onto food that has become susceptible to impurity, and in this way they explained the custom accepted in the past of redeeming the money onto bread (Responsa of Rabbi Betzalel Ashkenazi 2; Tal Orot YD 1; see Mishpetei Eretz 15:16). And Rav Shmuel Salant was accustomed to redeem ma'aser sheni coins onto a piece of sugar. Some argued that sugar is not food but a seasoning. And Har Tzvi (Zera'im 1:116:8) replied that for this purpose it is considered food. So too wrote Minḥat Shlomo (vol. 3, 151). And some argued that it is susceptible to impurity. However, the accepted custom in Jerusalem was to redeem onto sugar, as Rav Tukachinsky and Rav Eliyahu wrote. And so Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach did at first, and afterward he ruled that it is preferable to redeem onto a piece of potato. End of quote. (Today it is not clear that an ordinary piece of potato or a teaspoon of sugar is worth a peruta, and one must redeem onto a quantity that will certainly be worth a peruta.) When one redeems onto wine or oil, le-khatḥila it is good to pour them onto the ground (not for the sake of fertilizer), since with the sink there is some disrespect, as it goes down to the sewer. But when this involves effort, one may pour it into the sink, but not into the toilet, just as one should not place food in the garbage bin without wrapping.

Some questioned the text accepted in Israel and introduced a stringency to say "it and its fifth shall be deconsecrated onto a peruta and a quarter," since there are cases in which one is exempt from the fifth or obligated in it only by rabbinic law, and if they say, as is customary, "it and its fifth shall be deconsecrated onto a peruta," the principal that requires redemption will be redeemed for less than a peruta (Ḥazon Ish, Demai 15:11). However, the overwhelming majority of the poskim were not concerned about this, because whenever the redemption is made onto a peruta it takes effect, even if he intended to include the fifth and other components that are unnecessary. For he did not intend that the ma'aser sheni take effect on part of the peruta and the other components on the other part; rather, the ma'aser on the whole peruta, and the other components also on the whole peruta. For in any case the peruta is not the true value of the produce. And this has been the custom for generations, to redeem onto a peruta of the coin without any addition, and so wrote Maharḥu (Rav Ḥayim Vital) in Sha'ar Ha-mitzvot, Parashat Vayelekh; Olat Re'iya vol. 1, p. 353; Ḥazon Ovadya, Terumot U-ma'asrot p. 190; Rav Eliyahu in his siddur, and many others.

sections.title_en: One Does Not Redeem When the Value Is Less Than a Peruta, Nor in Jerusalem
sections.body_en:
If the value of the "ma'aser sheni" is less than a peruta, it is impossible to redeem it (Bava Metzia 53b), because whatever is worth less than a peruta has no significance such that an act of acquisition or redemption can be performed with it. And since it is impossible to redeem it, and it is also forbidden to eat it, destroy it or treat it with disrespect, one must wrap it and place it in the garbage bin, as is done with terumot. And one who wishes to be lenient can decide in his mind that as far as he is concerned it is worth a peruta, and redeem it onto a peruta. But the idea of a "peruta ḥamura" (stringent peruta) is strained and of no benefit, and therefore one should not use it, as explained in the note.17

One does not redeem pure ma'aser sheni produce in Jerusalem, that is, within the ancient walls of sanctified Jerusalem, including the City of David and Mount Zion, which were within the walls.18 For the whole reason the Torah permitted redeeming produce for money is in order to bring it up to Jerusalem, as it is stated (Devarim 14:24-25): "And if the way be too long for you, so that you are not able to carry it … then you shall turn it into money, and bind up the money in your hand, and go to the place which the Lord your God shall choose"; from here [we learn] that if the produce is already in Jerusalem – it is forbidden to redeem it. And if he redeemed it – the redemption is void (Yerushalmi Ma'aser Sheni 1:3; Rambam 2:4; Yeshu'ot Malko). Rather, he should place the "ma'aser sheni" produce that he separated in Jerusalem in a hidden place until it rots, and if it is a small amount, he should wrap it and place it in the garbage bin, as is done with terumot.19

notes_en.en:
Simply, ma'aser sheni worth less than a peruta should be buried in the ground, or wrapped and placed in the garbage bin in a manner that it will not be treated with disrespect. And the Ḥazon Ish (15:12) introduced the novel idea that one may be lenient to redeem less than the value of a peruta onto a coin onto which a peruta has already been redeemed, based on the words of Ḥizkiya (Bava Metzia 52b), that if one has already redeemed produce onto part of a coin, one may afterward redeem less than the value of a peruta, according to its exact value, onto the remainder of that coin. For since it is impossible to pin down the exact value of ma'aser sheni produce, the one redeeming intends to redeem it onto a coin worth more than its value, and onto the remainder in that coin one may redeem even less than the value of a peruta. And the first peruta must be at the highest level of obligation, because if it is at the level of obligation of two rabbinic factors it cannot be effective for a redemption at the level of obligation of one rabbinic factor (based on Bava Metzia 53a); therefore one should redeem the first peruta from ma'aser sheni of species whose obligation is of Torah origin and that a person grew for himself, such as grapes that a person grows in his garden (above 8:1), and this peruta is called a "peruta ḥamura." And even when they redeem all the perutot of the coin onto one peruta of another coin, they should leave that "peruta ḥamura," so that it will be a basis for redeeming produce that is not worth a peruta. And after bi'ur ma'asrot, they must again create a peruta ḥamura that will be a basis for the other redemptions (Mishpetei Eretz 15:11-12; 19).
The Ḥazon Ish sent a question on this matter to our master Rav Kook (Mishpat Kohen 53), and the Rav rejected his reasoning, because the possibility of redeeming less than the value of a peruta onto a coin onto which the value of a peruta has already been redeemed is on condition that the first time, produce worth at least a peruta was redeemed for its true value within the coin; for then there is a connection between the exact value of the ma'aser sheni in the coin and the remainder in the coin, which is the residue of the exact price. But today, when one redeems onto exact perutot within the coin, there is no connection between one peruta and another within the coin, and the remainder is not considered the residue of the peruta onto which ma'aser sheni was redeemed. However, our master Rav [Kook] wrote (there 54) that in pressing circumstances one may rely on those who hold that it is permitted to redeem ma'aser sheni worth less than a peruta, and all that Ḥizkiya said is that one does not add a fifth to it; and so it is implied by the Rambam (Hilkhot Ma'aser Sheni 5:4). So too wrote the Kesef Mishneh and the Gra, that according to Rashi and those who agree with him one does not redeem less than the value of a peruta, but according to the Rambam and those who follow his approach, one redeems even less than the value of a peruta. And so is the opinion of Rav Ovadya of Bartenura and Rabbi Eliyahu of Fulda. Furthermore, in another country this fruit is expensive and the ma'aser sheni is worth a peruta, and one may go according to the rate in that place (as explained in Kiddushin 12a; and in a rabbinic law one attributes leniently, as explained in Shabbat 151a). End of quote. And one should add that some hold that all that was said – that one should not redeem less than the value of a peruta – refers to [redeeming it for] less than the value of a peruta, but if the one redeeming agrees to redeem the fruit that is not worth a peruta onto a peruta, the redemption takes effect. And so it is implied by the Ramban, Bava Metzia 53b, and so is the opinion of Rabbi Akiva Eiger. Thus, in practice, in pressing circumstances one may redeem less than the value of a peruta. And according to the essential law one could rule so le-khatḥila, since the mitzva today is rabbinic, and a rabbinic doubt is treated leniently. It turns out, then, that one who wishes to be lenient may redeem ma'aser sheni that is not worth a peruta onto the value of a peruta, but le-khatḥila he should not redeem less than the value of a peruta, but rather store it away as one stores away terumot. And one who wishes to be meticulous should store away even ma'aser sheni that is not worth more than four perutot, for some say (Bava Metzia 53b) that whenever the value of its fifth is not a peruta, it is impossible to redeem it. So too wrote Olat Re'iya vol. 1, p. 350, and Minḥat Shlomo (3:152).

Shevu'ot 14a-b, Mishna: "… One may add to the city and to the Temple courtyards only with a king and a prophet, the Urim and Tumim, a Sanhedrin of seventy-one, two thanksgiving offerings and song; and the beit din walks, with the two thanksgiving offerings after them, and all Israel after them…" And in the Gemara there, 16a, it is explained that according to Rav Huna, the city is sanctified only if it was sanctified with all of these, and therefore in the days of Ezra they did not add to the area that was sanctified in the days of the First Temple; and according to Rav Naḥman, even if it was sanctified with one of them it is sanctified, and the first sanctity lapsed, and in the days of the Second Temple they sanctified it a second time with an eternal sanctity. According to the Rambam (Hilkhot Beit Ha-beḥira 6:14), the halakha follows Rav Huna, and therefore the boundary of the walls of Jerusalem is according to the walls in the days of the First Temple, which included the Temple Mount, the Jewish and Armenian Quarters and Mount Zion, which is outside the [present] walls, as well as the City of David down to the Shiloaḥ. But the Christian and Muslim Quarters are not in the area that was sanctified. And our master Rav Kook (Mishpat Kohen 96:6) is concerned also about the boundary of the wall made in the days of the Second Temple, since perhaps what the Rambam wrote is that one does not receive lashes for what was added in the days of the Second Temple, but by rabbinic law the wall of the Second Temple is also binding. Presumably his intention is to be stringent within the bounds of what is called "the Second Wall," which is the wall built by the last of the Hasmonean kings, which also includes most of the Muslim and Christian Quarters. But not the boundary of the Third Wall, which was completed at the end of the Second Temple period, and which reached as far as the Third Wall Street (Ha-ḥoma Ha-shelishit Street) at the border of the Me'ah She'arim neighborhood. And according to Rav Tukachinsky ("Ir Ha-kodesh Ve-ha-mikdash" 2:3:2-3), everything within the present walls is included in the prohibition, because the walls of the First Temple period also reached there. And so ruled Rav Eliyahu. In practice, one must be stringent in the area of the Temple Mount, the Jewish Quarter and the Armenian Quarter, Mount Zion and the City of David. And it is proper to be stringent in the entire area within the walls.

One who does not wish to leave the ma'aser sheni produce in Jerusalem until it rots should take the produce outside the boundary of the walls of Jerusalem, and separate terumot and ma'asrot there and redeem the produce as is customary. After the fact, if he brought it within the walls and it is difficult for him to take it out, he should first render the produce impure, by taking water, touching it with his hands so as to render it impure, and pouring it over the produce. In this way it turns out that he separates impure ma'aser sheni produce, and it will be permitted to redeem it, since it is in any case no longer possible to eat it there (Makkot 19b; Rambam 2:8; Mishpat Kohen 38:3).
